answer.rationale: 1. Why memory_c2 gets the verification: memory_c2 is the claim on which a switch to the low-cost primary vendor would rest. If it holds up, it validates that the incumbent's replacement candidate is viable on cost and operational integration. However, switching now, with the line at 94% of committed volume and zero buffer, introduces delivery risk during onboarding even if past onboarding was fast. memory_c2 says onboarding was quick, but the absence of any buffer at 94% load means any slip is unabsorbed. That risk outweighs the cost saving under the stated objective. memory_c3 (second-source resilience) is attractive but adds cost and is not needed while the line is stable; also, a second source does not address the 18% cut. memory_c6 (multi-year volume pricing) and memory_c4 (benchmarking at renewal) together point to a better lever: renegotiate the incumbent's terms. memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments already unlocked volume pricing, and memory_c4 shows benchmarking against market rates moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms. That combination is the cheapest path to the 18% target without introducing delivery risk. memory_c1 backs this: renewal kept integration stable across two cycles, no migration, no interruption. memory_c5 (deferring past quarter-end) is inapplicable here because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew; deferral would strand the line. 2. Why negotiate_terms wins on total cost of ownership and delivery risk: renewal preserves the incumbent relationship (memory_c1: stable integration, no migration, no interruption to scheduled deliveries), so delivery risk stays flat. Benchmarking against the low-cost vendor's rates (the existence of memory_c2's vendor is itself a negotiation lever) pressures the incumbent to match or beat on price, as memory_c4 shows they moved on price and payment terms before. Extending to a multi-year term at renewal (memory_c6) can push unit cost lower without narrowing service scope. This directly addresses the 18% spend cut. A second source (memory_c3) is retained as a future cycle item if the line's load rises or the incumbent's performance falters, but is deferred. Deferring the decision entirely is not viable because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, and the assembly line has no buffer. Switching the primary vendor, while cheaper per unit per memory_c2, carries onboarding and transition risk that cannot be absorbed at 94% utilization with zero buffer, violating the no-increase-in-delivery-risk constraint.
